34: WWI is fought for democracy and self-determination; Indians fight and die. Swadeshi, Ghadar, Home Rule and the Lucknow Pact add pressure. Swaraj now has moral weight.
Montagu tells the Commons on 20 August 1917: gradual steps towards responsible government within the Empire, timeline in British hands. Swaraj is no longer seditious.
Montagu tours the provinces and writes a joint report with Chelmsford 16-21 (1918). The Report is the blueprint, the Act is the law; together the Montford Reforms.
The Centre gets two houses for the first time: CLA (~145, 3 years) and CoS (~60, 5 years), elected majorities, direct elections. Gaya 'End or Mend' 1922 leads INC to 1923 polls.
Vote stays tied to income and property; no adult franchise. Women: PLCs may drop the sex bar, same property bar, under 1% qualify. Husband's-property rule comes in 1935.
Separate electorates for Muslims from 1909 become watertight, then extend to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians and Christians. Depressed Classes get nominated seats. Britain uses this for Divide and Rule.
Subjects are split Centre and Provinces with no lists, so the Centre can take any back. Viceroy keeps veto, 6-month ordinance and 75% non-votable budget. VEC: by convention 3 Indians of 8.
ICS exam also held in India (first 1922); Section 96C creates the Public Service Commission (1926, Ross Barker); 33% Indians promised gradually. Narendra Mandal 1921: advisory body for Princes.

Provincial subjects split: Reserved (Police, Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, Irrigation, Control over Officials) under the Governor; Transferred (health, education, local government, agriculture) under ministers answerable to the PLC.

Ministers have no money (Finance is Reserved) and no control over officials; the Governor can overrule them and take over Transferred subjects. Failing, they lose public trust, delaying responsible government.

Six grounds: subjects not federal, Dyarchy mocks federalism, no adult franchise, no responsible Centre, seats by importance not population, no effective self-government. Better than 1909, far from Swaraj.
35: Young barrister Gandhi comes for a Memon Muslim merchant's case. He is ejected from a first-class compartment at Pietermaritzburg despite a valid ticket, and resolves to fight.
The Indian community is leaderless and has no educated advocate. He alone can fight within the system, so a short visit becomes twenty-two years (1893 to 1915).
Franchise Amendment Bill 1894 strips Indians of the vote. Immigration Law Amendment Bill 1895 forces an indentured labourer to leave, re-indenture or pay a £3 a year poll tax.
He founds the Natal Indian Congress and Indian Opinion, and uses petitions, prayers and public meetings, a Moderate like the INC Moderates. The government is unmoved.

By 1906 he decides constitutional methods are not enough: the answer must be direct but non-violent. A Satyagrahi is truthful, non-violent, fearless, ready to suffer. Phoenix Settlement 1904 came from Ruskin.
Asiatic Law Amendment Act 1906: every Indian in Transvaal must carry a Registration Certificate. The promise to withdraw it is broken; he leads the RC bonfire and Jail Bharo.
Transvaal Immigration Restriction Act 1907 bars entry from Cape, Natal and Orange Free State. Indians cross illegally, refuse bail and hawk without licence; Gandhiji is jailed in 1908.
Tolstoy Farm (1910) becomes the base for Satyagrahis and their families. In 1912 Gokhale visits, the repeal promise is broken, and he advises two demands: abolish Poll Tax and RC.
The Poll Tax Campaign brings labourers in. A court recognises only Christian marriages, so other wives are not wives. Kasturba is arrested, 2,000 workers march, all workers strike.
Gokhale builds opinion across India, and Viceroy Hardinge 10-16 publicly condemns South Africa. Pressure from inside the Empire brings the government to the table.

The government concedes all three demands: Poll Tax abolished, RC dropped, Indian marriages validated. Gandhiji returns January 1915 having learned mass civil disobedience works; Champaran, Kheda, Dandi follow.
36: Politics rests on ideology. Gandhi is Father of the Nation because he brought all religions, castes, genders and regions into a movement for a Nation State: maximum contribution, not the only one.

Hind Swaraj (1909): ten-day sea voyage, Reader and Editor dialogue. Like Dayanand and Vivekananda he is a cultural nationalist, but goes further: dresses like the masses, uses Ram Rajya, Sita, Draupadi.

He criticises Western modernity built on industrial capitalism, profit and the coercive State, not reason or science. Indians enslave themselves to an alien system; he calls acts immoral (adharma), not just illegal.

Like Marx, his end-goal is a stateless society, through Enlightened Anarchism: morality over law, Village Republics, Gram Sabha (Article 243). Parliamentary democracy only a transition. Ambedkar answers: a strong State.
A village-based, self-sufficient economy like ancient India, rejecting the Industrial Revolution. Almost everyone else is pro-IR. Land by voluntary gift: Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan (Telangana, 1951).
Capitalists stay, under Trusteeship: the owner holds the enterprise for workers and community. Disputes go to Arbitration: both truths, then a middle path. It united Moderates and Extremists in 1920.

Satyagraha, truth-force: Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Constructive Work, Non-Violence, Morality. He never gains from the evil doer's weakness (backed Britain in both wars) and hates breach of promise (Montague 1917, Rowlatt Act 1919).
He starts light and escalates, but keeps the mass movement controlled: withdraws NCM after Chauri Chaura (22 policemen, February 1922). Constructive Work fills the truce, so S-T-S is really S-CW-S.

Satyagraha united Moderates and Extremists (Surat 1907), let common people join, and made repression a propaganda disaster. Swaraj stays undefined so each group finds its meaning; Jinnah and Tagore are uneasy.

Ruskin (1862) gave Sarvodaya and Phoenix (1904); Tolstoy (1894) non-resistance and Tolstoy Farm (1910); Thoreau (1849) civil disobedience; the Gita Nishkama Karma; Sermon on the Mount love of the enemy.

Nine fasts, Ahmedabad 1918 to Delhi 1948, incl. Epic Fast 1932 (Poona Pact, 71 to 147) and 1933 temple-entry. Papers: Indian Opinion 1903 to Harijan 1933. Ten arrests, 1906 to Quit India 1942; 1922 trial the only major one.
37: MG arrives January 1915, tours India on Gokhale's advice, stays out of the INM in WWI. Then three local fights: Champaran (Tinkathia abolished), Ahmedabad (50, 35, 27.5), Kheda (Patel joins).
February 1919: the ILC passes the Rowlatt Act against every Indian member, carrying Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime. MG, who hates breach of promise, calls a nationwide non-violent strike.

Leaders arrested, Punjab violence, O'Dwyer and Dyer's martial law. 13 April Jallianwala Bagh: 10 minutes of firing, 379 dead (official), 1,500 (INC). MG withdraws: control the INC, train people in non-violence.

Treaty of Sèvres (1920) strips the Khalifa; the Ali Brothers set up the Khilafat Committee (March 1919). Allahabad, June 1920: boycott launched. MG sees a Hindu-Muslim unity chance; Tilak, Pal, Besant, Jinnah, ML stay out.

Calcutta (Lajpat Rai): INC launches NCM, Swaraj promised in one year. Nagpur (C. Vijayaraghavachariar): MG takes over, Satyagraha replaces the pen; CWC of 15, linguistic PCCs, 4-anna fee make INC a mass body.
Tilak Swaraj Fund raises Rs 1 crore; the Reading talks fail. Peasants, workers, tribals join; imports halve. Prince of Wales visit in November 1921 turns strikes violent; MG confines CDM to Bardoli.
Police fire, 3 killed; the crowd burns 22 policemen. MG withdraws the NCM and passes the Bardoli Resolution: Constructive Work before any movement. Rowlatt repealed March 1922; Khilafat ends 1924.

Swarajists (Das, Motilal Nehru) want to end or mend the councils; No-Changers (Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Rajaji) want boycott. Gaya fails; Swarajists contest 1923; Gandhi-Das Pact, Belgaum 1924, makes them the parliamentary wing.

Swarajists demand a new constitution, civil liberty and help for industry, and use adjournment motions. No street support, Das dies 1925, ML lost, Responsivists split off; heavy loss 1926, INC leaves councils.

Constructive Work keeps cadres busy, unites communities, deepens rural hold, builds confidence, sets up national schools and panchayat courts. Passive Phase is anything but passive; Simon Commission 1927 rekindles the INM.
